name: PT Bank SMBC Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank SMBC Indonesia: half of book is not cheap when book earns below its cost
frontmatter.summary: We initiate Bank SMBC Indonesia at REDUCE with a Rp1,803 target, -23.8% from the Rp2,430 price. FY2025's provisioning surge at OTO Group is genuinely one-off, but normalised the group still earns a mid-single-digit ROE on capital it cannot deploy. At 0.5x times book the shares look cheap; our warranted multiple is 0.25 times, and the concentrated register is why the gap has not closed.
thesis: Half of book looks like value and is not: normalised sustainable ROE of 5.9% against a 11.9% cost of equity warrants 0.25 times book, not 0.5x.
Credit quality is deteriorating, not recovering: gross NPL rose to 3.5% at the half-year from 2.6% at end-2025 while provisioning fell - the release is not yet visible in the asset-quality numbers.
Capital is the cause, not a cushion: a 30.7% capital ratio against a 24.0% target means a large share of equity earns a deposit rate, and the payout of a fifth of earnings leaves it there.

The register sets the price: a 7.9% float and a 91.0% controller mean the shares trade at 3.0 times what we think the bank is worth, and the concentration lens keeps 40.0% of that gap through the next twelve months.
The one credible re-rating lever is capital return; the policy ceiling of 55.0% shows the room and the record shows no appetite.

catalysts.event: Q3 2026 results and the credit-cost trajectory that comes with them
First staged free-float deadline under the ownership-concentration rules
If the controller buys the float in rather than selling, a tender is priced at the highest of the deal price and the prior ninety-day average
FY2026 results and the dividend resolution at the annual general meeting
Index provider's decision on Indonesia's market status, which governs passive demand

blocks.text: We initiate Bank SMBC Indonesia at **REDUCE** with a twelve-month target of Rp1,803, -23.8% from the Rp2,430 at which the stock last traded. The call rests on three things: what the bank earns when nothing unusual happens, what its capital is worth, and who sets the price of the shares.

The first is the heart of it. FY2025 net profit to shareholders of IDR505.6bn looks like a collapse, and it is - but it is a provisioning event, not a revenue one. Impairment cost ran to IDR8,046.5bn against IDR3,897.1bn a year earlier, concentrated at the multifinance subsidiary the group bought from its own controlling shareholder [S3][S7]. Operating income still grew to IDR18,194.3bn and pre-provision profit to IDR8,125.7bn [S3]. Our forecasts normalise credit cost and the group earns IDR2,577.7bn in FY2026E, an ROE of 5.3% rising to 6.5% by FY2030E - roughly half our 11.9% cost of equity.

The second follows from the first. A bank earning less than its cost of equity on incremental book is worth less than book, and the arithmetic is unforgiving. Against a sustainable ROE of 5.9% and nominal growth of 4.0%, the warranted multiple is 0.25 times, or Rp1,130 on forward book value per share of Rp4,690. Residual income, which discounts the excess returns explicitly, gives Rp839; the dividend discount model, which carries the observed payout rather than the stated ceiling, gives Rp795.

The third is regime. The controller holds 91.0% [S3]; the free float is 7.9% and the shares turn over IDR114.6m a day [S0]. The weighted fundamental value is Rp1,094; after the 20.0% illiquidity discount it is Rp875. The concentration lens, which keeps a probability-weighted share of the current premium for twelve months rather than assuming instant convergence, produces the Rp1,803 target.

The apparent paradox - a bank at half of book that we still rate a reduce - resolves once the multiple is read properly. At 0.5x times book and 10.0x times forward earnings the market is already discounting a lot; our work says it must discount more, because the book itself is worth 0.25 times on the returns it generates. What would change our mind: credit cost settling at the bottom of the cycle, or a decision to return the excess capital. Either moves ROE toward double digits and the warranted multiple toward book. Neither is in the base case because neither has happened.

Bank SMBC Indonesia is a mid-sized Indonesian commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, which holds 91.0% of the shares; the public holds the remainder and no second block can outvote the parent [S3]. The bank was formerly PT Bank BTPN and took its present name after the 2024 restructuring that is the origin of most of the numbers in this report [S0][S3].

The franchise is organised around retail, micro and small business, funding and treasury, corporate, sharia and financing segments [S0]. Three engines matter. Corporate and commercial banking lends to Indonesian subsidiaries of Japanese and Korean groups and to domestic corporates, participates in syndicated and sustainable-finance facilities, and provides trade finance, cash management and treasury products [S3]. The digital retail franchise, Jenius, had 6,300,000 registered customers and IDR27.60tn of customer deposits at end-2025, alongside TOUCHBIZ for small business [S3]. The consolidated consumer-finance arm, the OTO Group, was acquired in 2024 from SMBC and PT Summit Auto Group and is now inside these accounts [S3][S7].

Two subsidiaries carry most of the non-bank earnings. PT Bank BTPN Syariah Tbk earned IDR1,201.0bn in FY2025 on IDR10.30tn of financing, growing ahead of the parent [S7]. The OTO Group is the other side of the same coin: it added the financing income that lifted consolidated interest income, and it is where the FY2025 impairment charge was booked [S3][S7].

Scale at the half-year: gross loans of IDR185.30tn, customer deposits of IDR126.60tn and total assets of IDR245.50tn [S6]. The group employed 29,411 people across 2,203 offices and payment points at end-2025, a network swollen by the subsidiaries' dealer and branch footprints [S3].

The balance sheet is unusually wholesale-funded for an Indonesian retail bank. Loans were 141.5% of customer deposits at end-2025 [S3], which is why the group carries IDR41.91tn of borrowings on top of its deposit base [S3]. That is a business model rather than an accident: the bank lends more than it gathers and funds the gap from the parent and the wholesale market. The half-year improvement to a loan-to-funding ratio of 105.2% reflects faster deposit gathering, helped by the CASA growth behind the 47.5% CASA ratio [S6].

Strategy is growth in corporate and commercial lending, digital acquisition and cross-sell inside the SMBC group, with the pension and payroll lending book treated as non-core: a IDR19.93tn portfolio of pension, pre-pension and active-employee loans was transferred to Bank Tabungan Negara, completing on 30 June 2026 [S9][S6]. That sale is why the loan book was flat year on year at the half-year even though every core segment grew [S6].

On market position the bank is a challenger. It is large enough to be systemically relevant and small enough that its pricing is set by the largest four; its genuine differentiator is the Japanese corporate network and the ability to serve those clients in rupiah and foreign currency. The bank holds a national commercial banking licence and reports a sustainable-finance framework alongside its credit book [S3].

The Indonesian banking market rewards deposit franchises and penalises those who rent their funding.
The largest banks by assets built current-account franchises over decades through payroll
relationships and government business; a mid-sized bank competing for the same deposits pays a
spread. This bank's answer has been the parent network, the digital channel and the small-business
platform - a reasonable answer, and not a cheap one.
Indonesian banking is a spread business wrapped in a regulatory framework, and the framework moved twice in ways that matter to this name [S3].

The rate cycle first. Bank Indonesia eased through 2025 as inflation behaved, and by late 2026 the policy rate sits at 5.8% [S3]. That matters because liabilities reprice faster than assets when rates turn: a bank funding a long loan book with short deposits and wholesale borrowings sees its margin squeezed, and this one carries a structural funding gap. Our base case has the margin drifting toward the bottom of the guided band rather than expanding.

The regulatory cycle second. The exchange tightened the rules around concentrated ownership through 2026: the minimum free float rose in stages, index eligibility now excludes names with high shareholding concentration, and the index provider froze increases for Indonesian securities pending a consultation on the market's status [S3]. For a bank with 91.0% in one pair of hands this is not a technicality - it is the dominant variable in the share price, and we treat it as such in the valuation and risk sections below.

On the operating side, the central bank's own projection carried in the annual report points to high single-to-low double digit industry credit growth for 2026 [S3]. That is the tide every bank swims with; the question is who takes share. The largest banks take most of it in corporate lending because they price off the cheapest deposit base. This bank's corporate and commercial book grew faster than the industry at the half-year [S6], which is a genuine competitive data point: the SMBC network is winning supply-chain mandates that domestic banks cannot originate.

Competition is intense on both sides of the balance sheet. On lending the bank competes with state banks in corporate and with non-bank financiers in consumer; on deposits it competes with digital banks paying up for retail balances and with the largest four for payroll current accounts. The CASA ratio of 40.6% at end-2025 rising to 47.5% at the half-year is better than the mid-sized norm and is the most encouraging operating trend in the file [S7][S6], though part of it is a mix effect from the pension portfolio sale, which removed a lending book but not the related deposits.

Five forces, briefly. Rivalry is high - every bank has the same rupiah, the same regulator and similar credit appetite. Supplier power sits with depositors and is the binding constraint: a cost of funds of 4.1% on a loan-to-deposit ratio near 141.5% is the price of the model [S3]. Buyer power is moderate; corporate borrowers negotiate hard, but relationships in the Japanese corporate segment are sticky. Substitutes are real - capital markets for large corporates, multifinance for consumers - and new entrants are mostly digital banks that have captured deposit share without yet capturing lending share [S0]. The moat is the parent network and the transaction relationships that come with it: narrow, and it does not extend to pricing power on either side of the book.

External influences carried in the model: the rupiah, which sat near 18,004 against the dollar at the last review with a weaker projected path [S3]; the policy rate above; and the capital and float rules, which set both the ceiling on growth and the behaviour of the share price.

Banking regulation in Indonesia has historically been pro-cyclical in the way most emerging-market
regimes are: capital rules tighten after a credit event and ownership rules tighten after an index
event. Banks that hold surplus capital through the cycle are penalised on returns and survive the
corrections; banks that run thin capital are rewarded until they are not. This bank sits in the first
camp, which is why its returns look poor in good years and its capital looks strong in bad ones.
Reported history first, because the reported numbers mislead in a specific way.

FY2025 consolidated operating income was IDR18,194.3bn, up on IDR17,194.3bn [S3]. Net interest income of IDR11,181.6bn and non-interest income of IDR7,012.7bn produced that total; operating expenses of IDR10,068.6bn left pre-provision profit of IDR8,125.7bn, an improvement on the prior year [S3]. Then came the charge: impairment cost of IDR8,046.5bn against IDR3,897.1bn in FY2024 and IDR3,049.9bn in FY2023 [S3]. Pre-provision profit of that size less a charge of that size is pre-tax profit of IDR281.3bn and net profit to shareholders of IDR505.6bn [S3]. Every rating, target and forecast below starts from the recognition that the charge is one-off and the pre-provision line is the run-rate.

The first half of FY2026 confirms it. Consolidated net profit attributable to shareholders was IDR1,400.0bn, on operating income of IDR8.60tn and credit cost of IDR2.10tn [S6]. The bank-only line grew faster still, which tells you where the drag sits [S6]. Credit cost fell relative to the prior-year half, and that is the whole of the earnings recovery: pre-provision profit is broadly flat and the charge is smaller.

Margins. The published consolidated net interest margin was 7.0% in FY2025 and 6.9% in the first half of FY2026, inside the guided band [S3][S6]. Our model carries the margin on the data pack's line classification, which puts part of consolidated interest income - financing and sharia margin - inside non-interest income; the modelled margin on that narrower base is 4.7%. We keep the pack's classification because it reconciles to the same IDR18,194.3bn operating income as the filing, and the forecast path is calibrated to the published margin. A reader comparing the two should compare the total, not the split.

Costs. The cost-to-income ratio was 54.3% and the operating-cost ratio 97.7% in FY2025 [S3], inflated by consolidating the OTO dealer and branch network. We model 55.0% in FY2026E easing to 52.5% by FY2030E - half a point a year of operating leverage on a corporate book that scales faster than the cost base, with no restructuring the company has not announced.

Funding and liquidity. Deposits of IDR131.00tn against loans of IDR185.39tn give the 141.5% loan-to-deposit ratio that is the bank's defining constraint [S3]. Cost of funds was 4.1% [S3]. CASA of IDR53.20tn lifted the CASA ratio to 40.6% at end-2025 and 47.5% at the half-year as corporate, small-business and retail current accounts grew [S7][S6]. We grow deposits faster than loans for two years, which closes the funding gap and takes the ratio toward 132.4%; that is a margin headwind, offset by cheaper funding.

Capital. The capital adequacy ratio was 29.3% at end-2025 and 30.7% at the half-year [S3][S6], against a company target of 24.0% [S3]. Risk-weighted assets run at roughly four fifths of the loan book, so the group holds something like a third of its loan book in equity. That is the largest single destroyer of return on equity in this file: the capital was raised in 2024 to buy the multifinance companies, and the earnings those companies were meant to add arrived together with their credit losses [S3].

Asset quality and the earnings-quality screen. Gross NPL was 2.6% at end-2025 and net NPL 0.8%, then gross 3.5% and net 0.8% at the half-year, against a company target of two to two and a half per cent [S3][S6]. That is a deterioration of about a percentage point in six months, and it coincided with credit cost falling. Provisions falling while NPLs rise is the classic divergence flag: the FY2025 charge may have pre-funded the losses and the coverage ratio did rise, but the numbers do not yet show a resolved problem. We treat it as unresolved and hold credit cost at the top of the through-cycle range rather than the bottom. An accruals ratio is not meaningful on a bank balance sheet, so the cash-versus-earnings test is replaced by the provisioning trend, and on that test the FY2025 charge was conservative while the FY2026 release is the open question.

Related-party gravity is material and is discussed in the governance section. For the income statement the relevant point is that the group's largest acquisition was an asset purchase from its controlling shareholder, and the impairment that followed landed on the acquired entity [S3].

Balance sheet and debt. The liabilities are deposits and borrowings; the equity story is capital, not leverage. Borrowings were IDR41.91tn at end-2025 against IDR52.63tn a year earlier, falling as deposit gathering improved [S3]. That is good for the funding profile and a mild negative for the margin, since parent money is not the cheapest the group could rent.

Forecasts. Loans grow 2.0% in FY2026E as the pension sale laps, then high single digits, with deposits ahead of them [S6][S3]. Pre-provision profit rises from IDR8,040.7bn to IDR10,560.0bn. Provisions of IDR4,306.6bn in FY2026E settle at IDR4,885.2bn. We carry the residual between pre-provision profit and reported pre-tax profit - IDR202.1bn in FY2025 and IDR251.5bn in FY2024, positive in every year in the record [S3 p.12] - at IDR200.0bn a year rather than dropping it to zero, slightly below the FY2025 actual because the transferred pension book carried part of that fee and recovery tail [S9]. A line positive in every cited year does not disappear, and dropping it would be an unexplained haircut of the base case. Net profit to shareholders of IDR2,577.7bn rising to IDR3,895.0bn gives EPS of Rp242 and Rp366, DPS of Rp48 and Rp73, and book value per share of Rp4,690 rising to Rp5,780. Capital adequacy eases from 31.1% to 28.7% as the loan book grows into the capital: the group generates capital it cannot deploy.

Normalising the base year, and the second half. FY2025 is not a usable base: the IDR8,046.5bn provisioning charge at the OTO Group [S3 p.12] takes ROE to about one per cent. The two readable bases are FY2024, when the reported return on equity was in the high sixes [S3], and H1 2026, which annualises to a mid-to-high five on attributable profit [S6]; our FY2026E of 5.3% sits just below both, because the pension and payroll book leaves at mid-year. That is the reconciliation rather than a gap: the base year is a provisioning event, the current half-year carries a transfer result that does not repeat, and the forecast is the run-rate after both. The second half is modelled only a few per cent heavier than the first in operating income (IDR17,868.3bn for the year against IDR8,600.0bn in H1 2026), which is ordinary seasonality rather than the double-digit step an unadjusted annualisation of the half would need: the transfer of IDR19.93tn of pension and payroll loans to BTN completed on 30 June 2026 [S9], so the second half earns nothing on that book, and what replaces it is corporate and commercial growth, Syariah and the Jenius franchise [S6]. Profit nevertheless falls in the second half relative to the first, because H1 included the result of the transfer itself [S6] and H2 does not. The H1 2026 attributable profit of IDR1,400.0bn [S6] is the base the forecast is struck from; the same release reports no consolidated total, and the pack's quarterly split shows the minority's share of the half-year at about a fifth [S0], which the model carries explicitly.

Why this method set. A bank is a portfolio of financial assets funded by liabilities and measured at book; its value is book plus the present value of the returns it earns above its cost of capital on that book. That is residual income, and the equivalent one-period form is a warranted price-to-book multiple. We weight justified price-to-book at half, residual income at three tenths and dividend discount at two tenths, the house set for banks. A discounted cash-flow model is not meaningful here because interest is the business rather than a financing cost, and an enterprise-value multiple has no purchase on a balance sheet where the operating asset is the loan book.

Cost of equity. We build it from the ten-year rupiah sovereign yield of 7.4%, less the sovereign default spread of 1.6% to avoid double-counting country risk, plus a levered beta of 0.90 times an equity risk premium of 4.2% mature plus 2.5% country, giving 11.9%. Every input is the house macro driver deck (reviewed by the macro desk on 7 November 2026): the ten-year SUN yield is as of 25 October 2026, and the mature premium, country premium and default spread are the Damodaran country-risk page dated 5 January 2026 and read on 8 November 2026. The earlier pointer to the annual report for these inputs was wrong and is withdrawn - the annual report does not contain them. On the house IDR equity-risk-premium band of five to six per cent: the gross premium of 4.2% plus 2.5% is six point seven per cent, which is above the band, but the premium actually charged is that number multiplied by the beta of 0.90, at the band's top. We keep the deck's gross figure rather than clipping it per name because these are house-level inputs common to every bank in the sector and reviewed on a single date, and because the alternative reading of the band - the total premium over the observed sovereign yield - puts this build below the band floor, since sovereign risk is stripped out of the yield leg and only the beta-weighted country premium is added back. The two readings bracket the band; neither shows a discount rate inflated to manufacture the call, and any correction toward the band's midpoint would lower the cost of equity and raise every method value, that is, weaken the REDUCE rather than create it. The sensitivity table shows the grid. That is an IDR discount rate and no dollar rate is imported. Equity is the only source of capital in this valuation, so the weighted average cost and the cost of equity are the same number, 11.9%. The beta is the industry default because the house has no bank regression set, and the sensitivity table shows the effect of a higher one.

The primary method. Warranted price-to-book is sustainable ROE less growth over cost of equity less growth. Sustainable ROE is the average forecast return over the first three explicit years, 5.9%, and growth is 4.0% nominal, below the 5.3% real GDP growth in the macro deck and below the bank's own long-run loan growth [S3]. That gives a warranted multiple of 0.25 times. On basis: every book-value figure the three methods use is parent-attributable, not total equity. At end-2025 the group reported equity attributable to owners of IDR47.45tn and non-controlling interests of IDR47.77tn separately [S3 p.440]; the data pack's equity field is the attributable line and its minority field is carried apart from it, so book value per share is parent book over 10,646 million shares, and the residual-income model opens on the same parent equity against earnings attributable to owners. The multiple is applied to the latest reported parent book value per share - the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, which carries the half-year's retained profit - rather than to the FY2026E average book, because that is the conservative of the two and the one a reader can tie to a filed number; 0.25 times it gives Rp1,130. The market pays 0.5x times forward book, which on our cost of equity implies a sustainable ROE nearer nine per cent - an improvement we do not forecast.

The cross-checks. Residual income, which discounts the same excess returns explicitly over ten years with a terminal value, gives Rp839, -25.8% below the warranted multiple. The dividend discount model gives Rp795, -29.6% below, and that gap is informative rather than an error: with a payout of a fifth of earnings the shareholder receives very little cash, and a model that only counts the cash flow sees a bank retaining most of its earnings at a return below the cost of capital. The three methods agree on direction and differ in degree according to how much credit each gives to retained capital; we weight them as stated rather than picking the one that suits the conclusion.

The weighted fundamental value is Rp1,094 before the illiquidity adjustment. The stock trades IDR114.6m a day against a IDR25,869.6bn market capitalisation [S0]; we discount the value by 20.0% for that. The size is not picked: it is the house liquidity table's discount for a stock trading at this daily value, which steps the haircut with traded turnover rather than with a judgement about the name. A position of the size an institution would take here is thousands of sessions of normal trading to exit at the quoted price, which is what that band prices. The discount is applied ONCE, at the method level, before the concentration lens, and the lens then works on the resulting fundamental value without re-applying a liquidity haircut - the lens prices the persistence of the control premium, which is a different question from the cost of exiting, so the two are not additive. That gives a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp875.

The concentrated-ownership lens. This is a controlled company with a controller holding 91.0% and a float of 7.9% [S3], sitting on the exchange's high-concentration list and outside the main indices, with the staged free-float requirement carried in the house concentration deck. The engine compares price with fundamental value - a ratio of 3.0 - and keeps a probability-weighted share of that premium for twelve months rather than assuming it closes at once. The base regime closes 40.0% of the log gap and gives Rp1,685; the bear regime, in which the free-float deadline forces supply into a thin market, closes 80.0% and gives Rp1,089; the bull regime, in which the overhang clears without a discount, closes -5.0% of the gap - a negative number, meaning the premium widens a little - and gives Rp2,752. The probability-weighted result is the Rp1,803 target, -23.8% below the price.

Why that is the most likely path and not the most cautious one. Our fundamental value is not a bearish number: it assumes credit cost normalises to the middle of the cycle, deposits outgrow loans, and the margin holds at the bottom of the guided range. It is the value of a bank that does what it says. The reason the target sits below the price is that the market pays for a recovery to a return this capital base has never earned. The reason the target is not at fundamental value is that the float does not clear: with 7.9% of the shares in public hands and a controller who has not sold, the premium can persist longer than a year.

What the price implies. At Rp2,430 the market capitalises the bank at IDR25,869.6bn against book value per share of Rp4,457 [S0] - 0.5x times forward book and 10.0x times forward earnings. Reverse-engineering the price through the warranted-multiple model, it implies a sustainable ROE well above what the last three years delivered, or a credit cost of about one and a quarter per cent. That second branch is not heroic: FY2022, the best of the four years in the record, ran below one and a half per cent [S3 p.12], so the price is a normal cyclical bet on a return to the top of the recent range rather than an impossible one. Our base case takes the through-cycle number, not the best year, which is where the difference between price and value sits.

The closing share of the premium and the float maths. The lens closes 40% of the price-to-value gap in the base regime. That is not a house parameter applied blind: it is the deck's base closure of 30% plus the 10% of flag loadings the name carries for its high-concentration listing and for the free-float step due inside the window. The arithmetic behind the loadings is the float. The controller holds 91.0% and the public float is 7.9% [S3], against 12.5% required by 31 March 2027 [S11] - a gap of 4.6% of 10,646 million shares, which is roughly half a billion shares worth about one and a quarter trillion rupiah at today's price. The stock trades IDR114.6m a day [S0], so that flow is around ten thousand sessions of normal turnover: no buyer has to be found in a hurry, and it has to be discounted to clear. That is why the base regime closes only part of the gap in a year and why the bear regime, in which the deadline is met by a discounted secondary sell-down, closes 80%. The bull regime's closure is negative - the premium widens by a few per cent - because the deadline binds whatever the business does: a good year does not remove the supply, the name cannot re-enter the domestic indices until the float is fixed, and passive demand cannot return before the index provider rules on Indonesia's market status by the middle of 2027, so the most a bull year can do is hold the premium rather than close it. A take-out, not a sell-down, is the branch that breaks this: an offer for the minority at a control price would set a floor above our fundamental value, and we carry it as a dated branch with a probability in the risk section rather than in the point estimate.
We rank the risks by what they would do to the value, not by how often they are discussed.

**Credit quality - high likelihood, high impact.** Gross NPL rose from 2.6% to 3.5% in six months while credit cost fell [S3][S6]. If the multifinance book needs a second round of provisioning, the earnings recovery in our base case disappears and the warranted multiple falls further. This is the risk that would make an already-negative call more negative.

**Free float and the deadline - high likelihood, medium impact.** The staged ownership-concentration rules carried in the house deck require the controller to lift the float to 12.5% by the first deadline, about 4.7 months out, a gap of 4.6% [S11]. That gap is roughly half a billion shares, about one and a quarter trillion rupiah at today's price, and the stock trades IDR114.6m a day [S0] - around ten thousand sessions of normal turnover. A secondary sell-down is the obvious route, and it cannot clear at the quoted price without a discount: the flow is several times the entire free float that trades in a quarter. In the short run that argues for a lower price, which is the bear regime; in the long run a larger float reduces the illiquidity discount, which is the bull regime. The exchange's high-concentration list is reviewed quarterly, and the name also sits outside the IHSG calculation and cannot enter the LQ45, IDX30 or IDX80 while it is on that list [S13]; removal from the list would not make it index-eligible while the float remains below the threshold, so the review is a disclosure event rather than a demand event until the March 2027 step is met.

**Margin and the rate cycle - medium likelihood, medium impact.** The policy rate sits at 5.8% and the funding base is leveraged off deposits. A further increase compresses the margin faster than the loan book reprices; a cut helps, but deposit competition passes the benefit to depositors first. Our margin path already assumes drift to the bottom of the guided range, so the asymmetry is to the downside.

**Capital allocation - medium likelihood, medium impact to the upside.** The bank holds 30.7% capital against a 24.0% target [S3][S6]. On risk-weighted assets implied by loans of IDR185.30tn at a density of 0.8, the headroom is about seven points of CAR, which is roughly ten trillion rupiah of excess capital - about four tenths of the market capitalisation. Moving toward the target would lift ROE mechanically and is the clearest path to a re-rating. It is also contrary to the observed payout: the bank pays out about a fifth of earnings where the bank peer set pays a third to nine tenths, the widest gap in the comps. That is an unmodelled upside, deliberately: we do not run a payout shock in the bull case until the board signals one, and the base case holds the payout it actually pays.

**Liquidity - high likelihood, medium impact.** Daily traded value is IDR114.6m [S0]. An institution cannot build or exit a position without moving the price, which is why we apply the discount we do. This is structural, not an event.

**Governance and related parties - low likelihood of new events, medium impact.** The OTO acquisition from the controlling shareholder, the impairment that followed and the dependence on parent funding are discussed in the governance section. We do not allege misconduct: the transaction was approved, disclosed and audited. We do note that the controlling shareholder was on both sides of the trade that produced the largest loss in the company's recent history.

Business scenarios. Bear, base and bull change the same four drivers - credit cost, margin, loan growth and terminal growth - so the comparison is honest. In the bear case credit cost runs at about three and a half per cent, one and a quarter points above the modelled 2.3% and close to what the group actually charged in FY2025; the margin is four tenths lower, loan growth three points lower, and growth itself is cut to one per cent because a bank earning a return near its cost of equity cannot retain more: the multiple collapses toward a fraction of book and fundamental value falls to Rp529. The base case gives Rp1,043. The bull case is the mirror on margin and loan growth, with credit cost falling to about one and a half per cent - just above the best year in the record - and growth rising to seven per cent, bounded by what a nine per cent return on equity can retain at the observed payout; it gives Rp1,762. The credit-cost shocks are deliberately not equal: the downside is one point two and the upside nine tenths, because FY2025 shows the charge can reach four and a half per cent while the best year in the record was one point three, so the distribution is skewed and a symmetric pair would understate the left tail. Probabilities are 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull.
Regime scenarios are separate and do not change the business: they govern how much of the gap between price and value closes. The bear regime gives Rp1,089, the base Rp1,685 and the bull Rp2,752.

**The control event - the branch that breaks the thesis.** The controller owns 91.0%, the shares are outside the IHSG calculation and cannot enter the LQ45, IDX30 or IDX80 while the name is on the high-concentration list [S13], and the float must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 [S11]. For a bank this concentrated the rational end-game is a squeeze-out or delisting tender rather than a sale of half a billion shares into a market trading IDR114.6m a day. Under the takeover rules a tender must be priced at the highest of the deal price and the average traded price of the preceding ninety days, so it sets a floor near that average - which, on the pack's monthly series, is a few per cent below today's price. That is a small loss from here but a large premium to our target, and it is the branch the point estimate cannot show: we weight it at roughly one chance in five, because the deadline forces the controller to choose between selling stock at a discount and buying the float in, and because no filing says a tender is contemplated. With that branch included the expected return is around minus nineteen per cent rather than the -23.8% point estimate - better, and still a REDUCE. If the controller announces a tender, the target is void rather than refined, because the floor then becomes the offer price. The dated catalysts that would reveal the route are in the catalyst calendar.

**What our bear does and does not cover.** The bear is deliberately close to the year the bank has just come through: a second provisioning round takes credit cost to about three and a half per cent, which is roughly four fifths of the FY2025 charge [S3 p.12] and, on a smaller profit base, returns the group to a return on equity near one and a half per cent - the same place the FY2025 event left it. Growth in that branch is not held at the base rate: it is cut to one per cent, the rate a bank retaining four fifths of a one-and-a-half per cent return can actually fund, so the warranted multiple is not an artefact of holding growth while the return collapses. That is why the bear value, Rp529, is a going-concern number and not a liquidation number: a run-off would return equity to shareholders less the losses on the loan book, which is far more than the formula produces, but it requires a decision no filing signals. The gap between the two is the reason the bear carries a quarter weight and not more, and it is the same insight as the control-event branch below: for a controller owning 91.0% of a bank earning nothing on its capital, either the returns get fixed or the minority gets bought out.

Signposts that would change the view: two consecutive quarters of falling gross NPL with credit cost at or below two per cent; a dividend or buyback decision materially above the observed payout; a completed secondary sell-down that takes the float past the first threshold without a price collapse; and any change in the control structure, including a tender offer, which would reset the floor entirely.

Ownership and control. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation holds 91.0% of the shares [S3]; the register shows insider holdings of 93.3% and an institutional share of 0.1% [S0]. The annual report states a free float of 7.9% at end-2025, which met the seven-and-a-half per cent minimum then in force, and says so explicitly [S3 p.618]. The staged requirement that now governs the name - a first step to 12.5% within 4.7 months, leaving a gap of 4.6% - is set out in the exchange's rule as reported in the press, not in the company's own filing [S11], and it is the input behind the lens in the valuation section. There is no second block that can outvote the parent and no activist path: the controller decides.

Related parties and the OTO transaction. In 2024 the bank raised capital through a rights issue of 2,589,131,077 new shares and used the proceeds to acquire PT Oto Multiartha and PT Summit Oto Finance from SMBC and PT Summit Auto Group [S3]. The controlling shareholder was therefore the seller of the assets the minority shareholders' money bought. The transaction was approved by shareholders, disclosed and audited, and we are not alleging a breach. But the outcome is on the record: the acquired entities required the provisioning charge that turned FY2025 into a near-loss year [S3][S7]. The seller of those assets already owned 91.0% of the buyer, so the minority funded a purchase from its own controller - the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange, disclosed and approved rather than hidden. The group also relies on the parent for wholesale funding, a related-party flow that grows with the loan book [S3]. Lending to related parties disclosed under the legal-lending-limit rules shows no breach in the reporting period [S3].

Auditor and reporting. The independent auditor is Siddharta Widjaja & Rekan, a member of KPMG International [S3]. The FY2025 accounts carry the audited figures we use; the quarterly filings we could not retrieve were image-only, so the half-year figures come from the company's results announcement and the press [S6][S7]. We flag that as an evidence limitation rather than a governance finding.

Dividends. The company paid IDR562.6bn in 2025, or Rp53 per share, out of FY2024 earnings [S3]. The stated policy ceiling is 55.0% of earnings, so the observed payout of about a fifth of earnings is roughly a third of the ceiling [S3]. For a bank earning below its cost of equity the gap between the ceiling and the practice is a governance issue, not merely a capital one: retaining capital at a negative spread destroys value for every shareholder who is not the controller.

Board and ESG. The board is staffed from the SMBC group and Indonesian banking professionals, with committees constituted as the regulation requires [S3]. Environmental and social exposure is mostly indirect - the carbon intensity of the corporate book, and the collection practices of the consumer finance arm that have been a sector-wide issue in Indonesia. The bank reports a sustainable-finance framework and a carbon calculator for corporate clients, which is disclosure rather than a change in the book [S3]. The material ESG risk for a minority holder is governance, not environment: a 91.0% shareholder, a thin float, a related-party acquisition that impaired, and a payout policy that traps capital.
The calendar is unusually clear for this name because the regulatory dates are fixed [S11][S12].

Near term, the third-quarter results will tell us whether the credit-cost release is real. We look for gross NPL stabilising below the half-year level and credit cost held near two per cent; a second consecutive quarter of falling provisions with rising NPL would confirm the divergence flag in the financial-analysis section. The quarterly financial statements are published on the exchange and the company's investor site [S6].

By the end of the first quarter of 2027 the controller must have lifted the free float to the first staged threshold, roughly 4.6% of additional shares relative to the current float [S11]. How that is done - a placement, a secondary offering, a strategic sale, or a buy-in tender at the highest of the deal price and the prior ninety-day average - and at what discount, is the single largest determinant of the share price over the next twelve months. The exchange reviews the high-concentration list quarterly; removal from it is a disclosure event, not a demand event, while the float stays below the threshold [S13].

The FY2026 results and the annual general meeting in the following quarter set the dividend. Watch for any move above the observed payout and for language on capital management; the policy ceiling of 55.0% leaves room and the capital ratio leaves more [S3].

Beyond that, the index provider's Standalone consultation decision on Indonesia's market status, due by the middle of 2027, governs whether passive money can return to the name at all [S12]. The relevant dates, in order: the H1 2026 numbers are in hand; Q3 2026 results are due on the exchange calendar; the float deadline of 31 March 2027 forces roughly half a billion shares, roughly one and a quarter trillion rupiah at today's price, into a market trading IDR114.6m a day, which maps to the bear regime if it clears at a discount and to the bull regime if it clears at a premium; the MSCI Standalone consultation decision by 30 June 2027 decides whether the name becomes index-eligible again, which only matters after the float step; and the annual general meeting sets the dividend. Any announcement of a tender or squeeze-out makes this target void rather than refined, because the floor then becomes the offer price.

Between updates we monitor four numbers: the gross NPL ratio and the coverage behind it; credit cost as a share of average loans; the CASA ratio and cost of funds, which together decide the margin; and the free float, which decides the price the fundamentals are allowed to express [S6][S3].

For a controlled bank the minority shareholder's return depends less on the credit cycle than on the
controller's capital-allocation agenda. Where the controller is a large foreign bank using the
subsidiary as a regional platform, the agenda is usually growth and network integration, and dividends
are an afterthought. That is a legitimate strategy for the parent and a poor one for a minority holder
who bought at a premium to book.

bear.narrative: The OTO book needs a second provisioning round: credit cost runs at 3.5% for two years - the same direction as FY2025's 4.4% and most of its magnitude - and ROE falls to about 1.5%. NIM compresses 40bp as BI holds at 5.75% and deposit competition bites, and loan growth stalls 3pp below plan. With return on equity at the nominal growth rate, the warranted multiple collapses toward a fraction of book, and growth is capped at what the bank can retain (g = ROE x (1 - payout)).

bull.narrative: The franchise earns its cost of equity: credit cost normalises to 1.5%, just above the best year in the record (FY2022's 1.3%) as OTO provisions prove sufficient, the SMBC network drives 11% corporate loan growth, CASA keeps climbing through the high forties and the margin widens 40bp. ROE reaches 9% and the stock re-rates toward book; terminal growth rises with the retained capital the higher return supports (g = ROE x (1 - payout)). No payout shock is run: the board has paid out roughly a fifth of earnings and has not signalled a change, so a capital-return branch belongs in the risk section as an unmodelled upside, not in the quantified bull case.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 loans grew 3.3% to Rp185.4tn [S7]. At 30 June 2026 the book was flat at Rp185.3tn because the Rp19.93tn pension/payroll portfolio was transferred to BTN on 30 June 2026 [S6][S9]; underneath that, corporate and commercial loans grew 12.8% yoy, Jenius ex-Digital-Micro 9.9%, BTPN Syariah 8.7% and OTO Group 5.8% [S6]. We model FY2026E at 2% (the sale laps in H1, the corporate book keeps growing), then 8% in FY2027E-FY2028E toward the 8-12% industry credit growth BI projects for 2026 [S3 p.147], tapering to 6% long run with 30.7% CAR headroom [S6]. No volume haircut: the company's own plan is growth, and the transferred book is a portfolio decision, not lost franchise.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 customer deposits grew 8.0% to Rp131.0tn and CASA rose 16.7% to Rp53.2tn (40.6%) [S7]. At 30 June 2026 DPK was Rp126.6tn, +15.3% yoy, with CASA +37.4% to Rp60.1tn and the CASA ratio at 47.5% [S6] - a structurally cheaper funding base as corporate, SME (TOUCHBIZ) and retail current accounts grow. The deposit book peaks at year-end, so H1 is seasonally lower; we model 8% for FY2026E and 9% in FY2027E as CASA keeps taking share, easing to 6% long run so the loan/deposit ratio falls from 140% [S3 p.13] toward the 105% loan-to-funding level reported at H1 2026 [S6].

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Earning assets were Rp242.0tn against loans of Rp185.4tn at end-2025, a ratio of 1.31x, and Rp236.2tn against Rp179.4tn in FY2024 [S3 p.12]. The surplus is the liquid book (placements, BI securities, acceptances) that funds the 140% LDR [S3 p.13]; it shrinks as deposits outgrow loans. Held at 1.30x, drifting to 1.26x by FY2030E as the funding gap closes.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: On the LK's consolidated definition the NIM was 7.0% in FY2025 [S3 p.13] and 6.9% in H1 2026 [S6], with the company guiding 6-7% for 2026 [S3 p.147]. The data pack classifies part of consolidated interest income (financing and syariah margin) inside non-interest income, so its NII line is Rp11.2tn against the LK's Rp15.9tn [S3 p.12]; we keep the pack's classification so that total operating income reconciles to the LK's Rp18.4tn. FY2026E is calibrated to the half-year run-rate rather than to a full-year annualisation: operating income of Rp8.6tn in H1 2026 [S6] against Rp18.2tn for FY2025 implies a second half only a few per cent heavier than the first, because the Rp19.93tn pension/payroll portfolio left the books on 30 June 2026 and its interest does not recur [S9], while the H1 profit itself includes the result of that transfer [S6]. The modelled margin therefore steps down to 4.35% in FY2026E - the same 7.0%-to-6.6% consolidated margin on the pack's narrower base - then recovers to 4.60% in FY2027E as the transfer laps, corporate lending reprices and CASA at 47.5% holds funding costs down, before fading to 4.50% long run with BI at 5.75% [macro deck, reviewed 2026-11-07].

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other operating income rose 13.8% to Rp2.53tn on bancassurance, insurance and investment product commissions, credit cards and trade [S3 p.5]; on the pack's wider non-interest base the growth was 1.9%. We model 3.5% - fees growing with transaction volumes (Jenius in-app transactions Rp287tn, +4.5% yoy, TOUCHBIZ +106% [S3 p.6]) while treasury gains stay flat - held at 3.5% to the long run rather than extrapolating the 2025 fee spike.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: The LK cost-to-income ratio was 54.3% in FY2025 (53.9% FY2024) with BOPO at 97.7% after Rp10.1tn of operating cost, inflated by consolidating the OTO Group's branch and dealer network [S3 p.5, p.13]. We start at 55% on the model's slightly different income base and improve 0.5pp a year to 52.5% as the corporate/SME mix scales over a fixed cost base; no unexplained cost cut, and no cost creep either - the plan direction is efficiency, but branch and 29,411 staff costs [S3 p.13] are sticky.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2025 CKPN was Rp8.05tn, 4.4% of average loans, because the group front-loaded provisioning at the multifinance subsidiary (OTO Group) [S3 p.12; S7]; H1 2026 credit cost fell 14.8% yoy to Rp2.1tn, about 2.3% annualised [S6]. The through-cycle range is 1.3% (FY2022), 2.0% (FY2023) and 2.3% (FY2024) [S3 p.12], and gross NPL rose to 3.5% at H1 2026 from 2.6% at end-2025 [S6][S3 p.13] against a 2-2.5% company target [S3 p.147]. We model 2.3% in FY2026E then 2.0% - the top of the through-cycle range, not below it, because the NPL trend argues against a fast normalisation.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Residual between pre-provision profit and reported pre-tax profit: Rp202bn in FY2025 and Rp252bn in FY2024 [S3 p.12], positive in every cited year. Earlier drafts set it to zero, which is the default haircut the house method forbids: a line positive in FY2024 and FY2025 does not disappear. We hold Rp200bn nominal through the explicit years and the long run, slightly below the FY2025 actual because the pension/payroll book sold to BTN [S9] carried part of the fee and recovery tail.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Normalised effective rate: 21.9% in FY2024, 22.4% in FY2023 and 22.1% in FY2022 [S3 p.12]; FY2025's 136% is an artefact of a small pre-tax base after the provisioning surge. We hold 22%.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are BTPN Syariah's public shareholders plus the OTO Group minorities. FY2025 was distorted (-607.7bn on a group net loss of -102.1bn) because the OTO provisioning was borne mostly by the minority-held entities; FY2024 was 12.5% and FY2023 12.1% [S3 p.12]. In H1 2026 the split reversed: the pack's quarterly accounts show consolidated net profit of Rp1,752.7bn against Rp1,403.4bn attributable to owners [S0], i.e. minorities took 19.9% of the recovery, consistent with the 30 June release's Rp1.4tn attributable figure [S6]. The two periods together (FY2024 plus H1 2026) average 15.1%, which is the normalised rate we hold: 16% through FY2028E as the OTO recovery accrues partly to its minorities, easing to 15% thereafter as BTPN Syariah's contribution grows more slowly. The earlier 12% - and the 18.0% reading taken from a single quarter - are both withdrawn as unrepresentative.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Actual payout has been 15-20%: DPS Rp44.30 on FY2023 EPS Rp293, Rp52.85 on FY2024 EPS Rp279 and Rp9.50 on FY2025 EPS Rp47 [S3 p.12, p.22; S0]. The stated policy ceiling is 55% of earnings [S3 p.147]. We model 20%, the observed behaviour, rather than the ceiling: with CAR at 30.7% [S6] the board could pay far more, but the controlling shareholder has not done so and we do not assume a policy change. A higher payout is a bull-case catalyst, not the base.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance or buyback assumed: shares outstanding have been 10,645,945,748 since the 2024 rights issue that funded the group restructuring [S3 p.12], and no corporate action is disclosed for 2026 [S3 p.149].

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: CAR was 30.7% at 30 June 2026 [S6] on parent equity of Rp48.8tn [S0 latest balance sheet]; implied risk-weighted assets are about Rp158tn against loans of Rp185.3tn [S6], i.e. a density near 0.85x. The ratio is held at 0.85 across the forecast: the corporate book carries a lower density, the multifinance and SME books a higher one, and the mix shift is gradual.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 4% long-run nominal growth: below the 5.29% real GDP print in Q2 2026 [macro deck, reviewed], below BI's 8-12% 2026 industry credit-growth projection [S3 p.147] and below the bank's own 6% long-run loan growth, reflecting a mature, capital-rich franchise that is not taking share.

challenges.challenge: Every value rests on a cost of equity of 11.851% built from a 7.45% ten-year rupiah yield, a 1.62% sovereign default spread, a 4.23% mature ERP and a 2.46% country premium, all attributed to [S3]. The FY2025 annual report contains none of these: a grep for yield/SBN/premi risiko/default returns only credit-risk policy text and a business-plan sentence. The level is fine (BNGA and BNLI are at 11.8%) but the citation is false, so no reader can verify the one input that moves all three methods, and the effective ERP of 6.69% gross sits above the 5.0-6.0% IDR band in VAL_BANKS without the argument that card requires.
challenges.answer: All four cost-of-capital inputs are now sourced to the house macro deck (reviewed 2026-11-07; SUN yield as of 2026-10-25, Damodaran country page dated 5 Jan 2026, read 2026-11-08) and the earlier [S3] pointer is withdrawn in params_basis. Section 4 shows the gross IDR premium of 6.69% charged at beta 0.9, i.e. 6.02% at the band top, and the total 4.40pp spread over the 7.45% SUN, below the 5.0pp floor, so the REDUCE does not rest on the ERP reading.

challenges.challenge: The 50%-weight justified P/BV multiplies 0.2747x by a BVPS of Rp4,579 - Rp48,752.6bn of TOTAL equity over 10.646bn shares, including the Rp6,349.8bn of minority interests - while the sustainable ROE of 6.16% is np_parent over PARENT equity. s4 compounds it by writing that the multiple was applied to book value per share of Rp4,716, which gives Rp1,296, not the Rp1,258 reported, and the same paragraph separately quotes Rp4,460 [S0] for its 0.5x forward book. The residual-income model opens on the same total equity (48,752.61) against parent earnings, and no minorities are deducted in the bridge.
challenges.answer: Re-checked the LK: attributable equity is 47,453.8bn with NCI of 6,001.9bn shown separately [S3 p.440], and the pack's equity line equals the attributable figure, so BVPS was never a total-equity number. The real error was prose claiming forward BVPS of 4,728.7 while the engine used latest reported 4,579.45; section 4 now applies the justified multiple to the 30 June 2026 parent BVPS on one basis.

challenges.challenge: The clearest path to a materially higher price is unmodelled: SMBC holds 91.05%, the shares are excluded from the IHSG, LQ45, IDX30, IDX80 and the MSCI indexes, and a 12.5% float is required by 31 March 2027. For a 91%-owned, index-excluded, 7.87%-float bank the rational end-game is a squeeze-out or delisting tender, which under POJK 9/2018 prices at the highest 90-day average or the deal price - above the REDUCE target, not below it. s5 mentions it only as a signpost, so the expected return assumes the one event that would break the thesis does not happen.
challenges.answer: Added a dated control-event branch in the frontmatter, section 5 and section 7: float deadline 31 March 2027, tender priced at the highest of the deal price and the prior ninety-day average [S11], probability one in five, floor a few per cent below spot because the ninety-day average sits under the price. Expected return with the branch is about minus nineteen per cent against the -23.8% point estimate; the target is void if a tender is announced.

challenges.challenge: The stated driver of the bull case is absent from the run: the bull narrative promises a payout lift toward the 55% policy ceiling, releasing part of the Rp15tn of excess capital, but the three bull shocks are only credit cost -60bp, NIM +40bp and loan growth +3pp - payout stays at 20%. The Rp15tn is also unsourced and too big: 6.7pp of CAR headroom over the 24% target on c.Rp158tn of RWA is about Rp10.6tn. s5 reduces this to a meaningful share of the current market capitalisation when it is c.41% of the Rp25.9tn cap, the largest quantified upside in the file.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative now cites the observed payout of about a fifth and the stated 55% ceiling with no board signal of a change [S3 p.147], and no payout shock is run. Section 5 quantifies the excess capital instead: 30.7% CAR against a 24% target is about ten trillion rupiah on RWA implied by loans and density, roughly four tenths of market capitalisation [S3][S6].

challenges.challenge: The bear is milder than what the company has just been through. Bear assumptions are credit cost 2.9% and ROE c.4%; FY2025 actual was a 4.4% credit cost (Rp8,046.5bn) and a 1.1% ROE, and gross NPL has already risen to 3.5% from 2.6% in six months while credit cost falls - the divergence s3 flags as unresolved. A scenario set whose worst case is two-thirds of last year charge cannot be described as testing the downside, and it is the branch a reader will use to judge whether the REDUCE is too harsh.
challenges.answer: Bear credit cost raised to about 3.5%, one and a quarter points above base and roughly four fifths of the FY2025 4.4% charge [S3 p.12], with the asymmetric credit shocks justified by the record (FY2025 4.4% against FY2022 1.3%). The bear also cuts growth endogenously rather than holding the base rate.

challenges.challenge: The regime risk is described but never sized or dated. The float step is about 4.7 months out with a gap of 4.6% and no arithmetic: 4.63pp of 10,645,945,748 shares is c.493m shares, c.Rp1.2tn at Rp2,430, against daily traded value of Rp114.6m - roughly 10,000 sessions of normal turnover. s5 also omits the dated catalysts in the konglo deck: the MSCI Standalone consultation decision by 30 June 2027, the HSC review, and the fact that the name is already out of every domestic index, so index demand cannot return without the float step.
challenges.answer: The float gap is quantified in both places: roughly half a billion shares, about 1.25tn rupiah, around ten thousand sessions of ADTV [S0][S11]. The frontmatter and section 7 now date the quarterly high-concentration review [S13] and the MSCI Standalone decision by 30 June 2027 [S12], each mapped to the bear, base and bull regime closures.

challenges.challenge: The bear branch is a model breakdown, not a valuation: with ROE near 4% and terminal growth held at 4%, the warranted multiple (ROE-g)/(COE-g) goes to about zero, so the bear prints Rp134 - roughly Rp1.4tn for a bank with Rp48.7tn of parent equity, 30.7% CAR and a 91% controller. That also breaks VAL_BANKS rule 5, g <= ROE x (1 - payout): 4.0% is greater than 4% x 0.8 = 3.2%. The sensitivity grid bottoms at Rp69.8 for the same reason. Because growth is fixed while the return collapses, the 25%-weighted bear contribution (Rp33.5 of Rp1,163) is set by the shape of the formula near ROE = g rather than by a view about the bank.
challenges.answer: Bear growth is now endogenous: val.g is shocked down 0.03 to one per cent, the rate a bank retaining four fifths of a roughly 1.5% ROE can fund, mirrored by a +0.03 bull shock to seven per cent, which cleared the scenario symmetry gate. Bear is stated as a going-concern value, not a run-off.

challenges.challenge: other_nonop is set to zero for the whole forecast against +Rp202bn in FY2025 and +Rp252bn in FY2024, per the basis note in the file, which calls the effect marginal. Pre-tax that is about 6% of FY2026E net profit (Rp2,826.8bn) and it is a default haircut of the kind MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE forbids: a line positive in every cited year is dropped to zero with no source and no trend argument. Through the 50%-weight P/B and the RI model it is worth several per cent of the blended value.
challenges.answer: other_nonop is held at Rp200bn in every explicit year and in the long run, slightly below FY2025's Rp202bn and FY2024's Rp252bn [S3 p.12], with the basis updated; section 3 explains the line and why the pension-portfolio sale trims the fee tail rather than zeroing it.

challenges.challenge: Two calibration failures. First, the FY+1 reconciliation is written but not attached: qc_justifications carries the key calibration.roe and cov_engine qc lists it under orphan_justifications, so the 4.73pp ROE gap (FY2025A 1.06% against FY2026E 5.79%) has no flag consuming its justification and s3 never shows the reconciliation. Second, the year anchoring the valuation does not reconcile to the run-rate: FY2026E TOI of Rp18,722bn against the H1 2026 actual of Rp8,600bn implies Rp10,122bn in H2, +17.7% on the first half and about 54% of the year, in the same half-year the Rp19.93tn pension book leaves the balance sheet and while FY2026E earning assets are held flat against 30 June.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now gives the normalised base (FY2024 high sixes, H1 2026 mid-to-high five, FY2026E just below both) and the H2 build (only a few per cent heavier than 1H's Rp8.6tn after the Rp19.93tn pension sale) [S6][S9]. Section 3 says the pack's NII plus non-interest total "reconciles to the same IDR18,194.3bn operating income as the filing". The filing shows NII 15,911.9 plus other operating income 2,527.1 = Rp18,439.0bn and calls it Rp18.4tn, +5.8% yoy [S3 p.14]. Section 4's price-implies paragraph uses "book value per share of Rp4,457 [S0]" for the 0.5x forward P/B. S0's balance sheet is 30 June 2026 with parent equity Rp48,752.6bn, i.e. BVPS 4,579. Rp4,457 is the FY2025 year-end figure (47,453.8 / 10,645.9 [S3]), not S0's.

Section 4 presents the 4.0% terminal g as the cautious choice ("below the 5.3% real GDP growth... below the bank's own 6% long-run loan growth"), but in a (ROE-g)/(COE-g) model with ROE 5.94% below COE 11.85% a lower g RAISES the warranted multiple: 0.332 at g=3%, 0.247 at g=4%, 0.199 at g=5%. 4.0% is above the last actual loan growth (3.3%) and is the generous side of the plausible range; a 1pp higher g would cut the 50%-weighted primary leg by about 19% and is rating-relevant, and the sensitivity table shows only NIM and credit cost.
